prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned prose, above all in Blinding and Solenoid, that turns memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of rare formal and imaginative scale.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one prize part, naming Mircea Cărtărescu (B031) alone. The grounds are the common literary criteria, not the fact that colleagues' round-1 files agree. A voice that is distinctive and recognizable, formal ambition carried across very large structures, and a continuing project in which memory, the body and dream become one imaginative world together give the oeuvre depth and scale. As far as public knowledge and translation allow me to judge, no other shortlisted writer combines these as clearly across a body of work spanning decades. The round-1 exchange sharpened how I hold the case, not what I conclude. On the chair's repetition question, my provisional reading is that Blinding, as I understand it, is a mythic, multi-layered, multi-volume construction. Solenoid, from public descriptions, is organized around a diary-like first-person narrator whose ordinary Bucharest life gives way to cosmological visions. If that description is right, the later book changes the mode of the project and does not merely repeat motifs. This is a claim from public description and translation. I have not verified it by close reading, and I would not want it treated as a finding. On the standard of sustained quality, I accept Sem-Sandberg's approach: a whole-oeuvre citation rewards the peaks and the overall direction, and does not demand uniform quality across every volume. The citation should still be honest about the fact that some late volumes may be weaker. On scope, I keep the citation centred on the prose and name the two works that carry the case. Poetry is a lyric foundation and context, because its translation coverage is the thinnest part of what we can evidence. If the committee prefers to name poetry, I would accept that only with explicit acknowledgement that this part is less well supported.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. The effect of dense, long-breathed Romanian prose reaches me only through translation, and translation may flatter or flatten it. The development-versus-repetition question cannot be settled from the supplied record. If a close reading or expert report showed that Solenoid and later volumes mostly restate the earlier architecture, or that the late digressive phase is uneven in a way that undermines sustained quality, I would move first to Tawada (B015) and then to Zurita (B005). A second concern is structural. All six round-1 files reach the same conclusion from the same public knowledge and the same translation limits, so shared blind spots are possible. The convergence is not evidence of merit, and I do not want to treat it as such. The late-phase unevenness concern is also only partly answered by the 'peaks and direction' standard. That standard is reasonable, but it places weight on exactly the judgement of peaks that none of us has verified by reading the Romanian.

responses.point: Mattson keeps Cărtărescu first but holds Michon and Wright as serious alternatives, for concentration of language and for reinvention of narrative form. She acknowledges that the repetition question and the thinner coverage of the poetry could weaken the case if close reading showed sameness in the later books. She also says she prefers the longer cumulative record over Michon's smaller corpus.
responses.response: I agree that the repetition question is the main risk, and I would not let Michon's alternative status become a reason to avoid testing it. In round 1 I said the committee had not yet explained why a few books suffice for a whole-oeuvre judgment. Her reply moves toward an answer: intensity is real, but a smaller corpus gives less to test for development and breadth. I accept that as a reason for preferring the larger record, not as a ruling that Michon's achievement is lesser. If she or another member wants to argue explicitly that a few books are enough, that argument would need to show what makes the small corpus complete and not just consistent. I have not heard it yet. For Wright I hold the same position as Mattson. Voice and structure are the literary case, and the political and cultural significance of her subject should stay separate from it. I would place Michon and Wright below my two named alternatives because their evidence base for sustained, developing achievement across a body of work is narrower. That is a judgement about the available evidence, not about their prose.

responses.point: Olsson treats recurrence of imagery in a metaphysical project as partly the method. He says what matters is whether later works, Solenoid in particular, change the architecture and not only the motifs. He also argues that translation risk falls mostly on sentence texture and less on the larger architecture, and he wants expert reports for the weaker-covered corpora.
responses.response: I agree with his reframing, and my answer to the chair's first question follows it: the test is architecture, not motif. I am more cautious about the second part of his argument. Large-scale structure is more translatable than sentence music, but not fully. Pacing, digression and the control of a very long sentence are part of the architecture in this kind of prose. I therefore hold my reading of Solenoid as provisional. His point about expert reports is the most practical response to the chair's translation question. I would want such reports for Romanian, and also for the Japanese and German corpora in Tawada's case. Her case is the one I would most want to test if the repetition concern proved well founded. I would also treat a report as a check on our readings and not as a replacement for the committee's own judgement.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that a citation rewards the oeuvre's peaks and overall direction, and does not require uniform quality. He would keep the poetry secondary in the citation. He ranks Zurita second and says the award would be for the written texts, so Zurita remains an alternative and not a stronger choice than Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I accept the peaks-and-direction standard and give it as my answer to the chair's third question. The citation should not claim that every late volume is equally achieved, and it should rest on Blinding and Solenoid. I agree on keeping the poetry secondary. I would also hold myself to the same discipline on Zurita, whom I keep as my second alternative. His case would have to rest on Purgatory and Anteparadise as written poems, with the landscape works treated as part of the practice and not as literary evidence. Where I add a caution is the claim that Cărtărescu's late work extends the earlier trilogy. He, Sward and I have each said this, and none of us has checked it by close reading. Saying it three times does not make it more verified. I would rather the committee record it as a shared provisional judgement.

responses.point: Carlberg warns that Nobel's 'idealist' direction is open to broad interpretation and could favour almost any serious writer, so she wants the case to rest on voice, form and imaginative depth. She also treats Tawada as her closest alternative and says the evidence of access to Tawada's two corpora is uneven.
responses.response: I agree with her on the 'idealist' criterion and answer the chair's last question the same way: the citation should rest on voice, form and imaginative depth, and not on a reading of the will that can be stretched to fit. If the committee wants the will cited for the sake of form, it can do so without making it a ground of merit. On Tawada, her statement that access to the two corpora is uneven matches my own uncertainty, and it is why Tawada is my first fallback and not my first choice. If the repetition concern weakened Cărtărescu, Tawada would be the writer whose formal invention, breadth across prose, poetry, essays and drama, and consistency of concern most fully meet the criteria. The citation would need to describe the work as written across two languages, without privileging either. That wording is easier to draft than to verify, and I would want the committee to say so openly.

uncertainties: My assessment rests on public knowledge and translation. I have not independently verified sources or read the full corpus of any candidate, and I cannot judge the Romanian prose directly.

Whether Solenoid and the later long works change the architecture of the earlier project or restate its imagery is unresolved. My reading of the difference between Blinding and Solenoid is from public description and is provisional.
Poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation, so a citation naming poetry would be only partly supported. I keep the poetry as context.
The late digressive phase may be uneven. The peaks-and-direction standard is reasonable, but it depends on a judgement of the peaks that rests on translation.

For the fallbacks, Tawada's wordplay across Japanese and German and Zurita's verse rhythm lose the most in translation, and the committee cannot read the Japanese and German corpora equally. Comparisons across languages are therefore uneven.
All six round-1 files share the same sources and the same limits, so the convergence on B031 may reflect correlated assumptions and not independent confirmation.
Carlberg's actual committee voting status is undocumented. The six-vote structure and the four-vote majority are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. None apparent from the supplied profile: it lists professional ties to committee colleagues, to a collaborator (Kate Larson) and to Selma Lagerlöf as a biographical subject, but no connection to any shortlisted writer. My own fiction, biography and essay writing are context only and are not treated as evidence of a preference for any candidate. I note the chair's disclosed scholarly overlap with Adonis and Tawada, since both are among the alternatives named in round 1. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
